title: The Quiet Craft of Diplomacy
text:
Diplomacy is often portrayed as a theatre of grand gestures, yet its most consequential work tends to occur in quiet, carefully choreographed exchanges between officials who rarely appear in headlines. Negotiators rely on a shared vocabulary of ambiguity, in which a phrase such as 'constructive engagement' can signal willingness without committing anyone to a particular outcome. Such deliberate vagueness is not evasion but a calculated tool for preserving face while leaving room for compromise. Historians have noted that many treaties endured precisely because their authors left certain questions unresolved.

The same ambiguity, however, can generate misunderstanding when parties read the same words in incompatible ways. A pledge of 'full support' may be understood by one government as a binding guarantee and by another as a mere expression of goodwill. Consequently, experienced envoys often insist on written clarification of key terms, even at the risk of appearing distrustful. In this sense, diplomacy is less about eliminating ambiguity than about deciding, deliberately, how much of it a relationship can safely bear.

According to the second paragraph, how might one government understand a pledge of 'full support'?
options: As a request for a meeting

questions.text: What does the author imply about experienced envoys who ask for written clarification?
options: They are mainly trying to end negotiations
They accept that appearing distrustful is a worthwhile risk

questions.text: What is the author's main view of the role of ambiguity in diplomacy?
options: It is a deliberate choice that must be managed
It only causes harm and never helps
It is mainly the result of poor translation

vocabulary.definition: the quality of having more than one possible meaning
an agreement reached when each side gives up part of its demands
official representatives sent to carry out negotiations for a government
an explanation that makes something easier to understand

paragraph_translations: La diplomacia suele presentarse como un escenario de gestos grandiosos, pero su trabajo más trascendente suele desarrollarse en intercambios discretos y cuidadosamente coreografiados entre funcionarios que rara vez aparecen en los titulares. Los negociadores se apoyan en un vocabulario compartido de ambigüedad, en el que una frase como 'compromiso constructivo' puede señalar disposición sin obligar a nadie a un resultado concreto. Esa vaguedad deliberada no es evasiva, sino una herramienta calculada para preservar la imagen y dejar margen para el compromiso. Los historiadores han señalado que muchos tratados perduraron precisamente porque sus autores dejaron ciertas cuestiones sin resolver.

Sin embargo, la misma ambigüedad puede generar malentendidos cuando las partes interpretan las mismas palabras de maneras incompatibles. Una promesa de 'apoyo total' puede ser entendida por un gobierno como una garantía vinculante y por otro como una simple expresión de buena voluntad. En consecuencia, los enviados experimentados suelen insistir en una aclaración por escrito de los términos clave, incluso a riesgo de parecer desconfiados. En este sentido, la diplomacia no consiste tanto en eliminar la ambigüedad como en decidir, deliberadamente, cuánta puede soportar una relación con seguridad.
